sections.h2: What is a transfer on death deed in Colorado?
sections.html:
Colorado calls it a beneficiary deed. It is a deed that names who receives a house when the owner dies, and under C.R.S. 15-15-401 it is subject to revocation by the owner and says the conveyance takes effect on the owner's death.

The person who signs is the owner, and the person named is the grantee-beneficiary. A successor grantee-beneficiary can also be named to take if the first choice does not survive the owner. The rules sit in Part 4 of Article 15 of the Colorado Probate Code, sections 15-15-401 through 15-15-415.

Many people look for a Colorado transfer on death deed because they want a house to skip probate. The statute says a beneficiary deed is not a will, and it cannot be thrown out for failing the formalities that apply to wills (15-15-412).

sections.h2: Which Colorado statute sections cover beneficiary deeds?
sections.html:
Part 4 of Article 15 holds the whole set of rules, and each section answers one question. The table lists the ones we read on the Justia copy of the Colorado statutes.

Justia warns that its copy may not be the newest version, so a final check against the official Colorado statutes is worth the few minutes.

sections.h2: What has to happen before the owner dies?
sections.html:
The deed must be recorded during the owner's lifetime with the county clerk and recorder where the house sits. Section 15-15-404 puts it in capital letters on the sample form: the deed must be recorded before the grantor's death to be effective.

A few other points from the statute:

  • No payment from the beneficiary is required, because the section says no consideration is needed.
  • The beneficiary does not have to sign, agree or be told before the owner dies, though the beneficiary may still disclaim the property.
  • The deed has to meet the notarization and acknowledgment rules in 15-15-406, which point to C.R.S. 38-35-109 and 38-35-101.
  • Unless the owner says otherwise, the deed carries no title warranties and works like a bargain and sale deed.

The sample form also tells the assessor and treasurer that the beneficiary's address is only for identification. Tax notices keep going to the owner while the owner is alive.

sections.h2: What does recording a beneficiary deed cost in Colorado?
sections.html:
Recording is a county charge, and the two county pages we opened both list a $43 fee per document. The Denver recording page and the Delta County recording page each give that figure.

Denver also asks for one-inch top margins and half-inch side margins on documents, and it says mailed documents can take 7 to 10 days while e-recording takes minutes. Other counties set their own fees and habits, so call the clerk in the county where the house sits before you mail anything.

Delta County states that death certificates and verification-of-death documents recorded in the real estate records have no fee. That matters later, when a beneficiary needs the death on record.

sections.h2: Can the owner still sell the house after signing the deed?
sections.html:
Yes. During the owner's life the beneficiary has no right, title or interest, and the owner keeps full power over the property without the beneficiary's signature, consent or notice (15-15-402).

That means a homeowner who recorded a beneficiary deed years ago can still list the house, take a cash offer, refinance or pledge it. A normal sale deed signed by the owner passes title to the buyer, and the old beneficiary deed has nothing left to transfer once the house is gone.

Sellers sometimes get stuck because family members believe the named beneficiary has to approve. The statute says the opposite while the owner is alive. If the owner has lost capacity, the question becomes who holds authority to sign, and that is a job for an attorney.

sections.h2: How do you cancel or change a beneficiary deed?
sections.html:
The owner signs and records a written revocation before death. Under 15-15-405 it must describe the property, revoke the deed, and be recorded with the clerk and recorder in the county where the property is located.

  • The beneficiary does not need to sign or be notified.
  • A new beneficiary deed for the same property revokes all earlier ones, even if it covers only part of the owner's interest.
  • If several deeds or revocations are recorded before death, the one signed most recently controls, whatever the recording order.
  • A will cannot revoke or change a beneficiary deed that follows the statute.

The will point catches families by surprise. A will that leaves the house to one child does nothing against a recorded beneficiary deed naming another.

sections.h2: How do joint tenants and Medicaid affect a beneficiary deed?
sections.html:
A joint tenant can use a beneficiary deed, but title passes to the named person only if that joint tenant is the last surviving joint tenant (15-15-408). The deed does not break the joint tenancy.

Medicaid is the other trap. Section 15-15-403 says a person applying for or receiving medical assistance cannot qualify while holding an effective beneficiary deed where the state could assert a repayment claim, and signing one while applying makes the property a countable resource.

Section 15-15-407 adds that the beneficiary's interest is subject to the state's claims to recover medical assistance payments. Anyone near a nursing-home or Medicaid decision should get advice before recording or leaving a deed in place.

sections.h2: What happens when the owner dies?
sections.html:
Title vests in the beneficiary only at the owner's death, and the beneficiary takes the owner's interest subject to existing liens, later interests and interests the beneficiary knows about (15-15-407).

If the house carries a mortgage, the loan stays with the house. A deed of trust the owner signed does not disappear because a beneficiary deed exists.

ItemRuleSection
Unrecorded interestsHolder must record a notice within four months after the owner's death15-15-407
Creditor claims against the ownerBarred one year after death15-15-411
Other claims by heirs or deviseesBarred at the earlier of three years after death or one year after the death is recorded in the county15-15-411
Medicaid recoveryBeneficiary's interest is subject to the state's claim15-15-407

Fraud is the exception to the time limits, since 15-15-411 does not bar an action to recover property obtained by fraud.

sections.h2: Can a beneficiary sell the house quickly after inheriting it?
sections.html:
Yes, once title has vested, the beneficiary can sell like any other owner, and a buyer or lender who pays value without notice gets protection under 15-15-410.

That section says such a buyer takes the property free of the rights of interested persons in the estate, and a recorded transfer that shows the state documentary fee is prima facie evidence the transfer was for value. The beneficiary stays answerable to the estate's personal representative for duties under 15-15-103.

In practice, buyers and title companies want to see the recorded beneficiary deed, proof of death on record, and a clean payoff for any loan.

If you inherited a Colorado house through a beneficiary deed and want to talk about selling it as is, call us for a written cash offer. Decisions about debts, other heirs and Medicaid recovery belong with an attorney.

sections.h2: Questions to ask before you rely on a beneficiary deed
sections.html:
• Is the deed recorded in the right county, and was it recorded before the owner died?
  • Was it signed and acknowledged to the standard in 15-15-406?
  • Does a later deed or revocation exist that was signed after this one?
  • Was the owner on Medicaid, or planning to apply?
  • Are there loans, tax bills or unrecorded claims on the house?

A title company can search the recorded documents for the answers to the first, third and fifth questions.

faqs.q: Is a beneficiary deed the same as a transfer on death deed in Colorado?
faqs.a: Yes. Colorado statutes use the term beneficiary deed, and it does the work other states call a transfer on death deed. It conveys the owner's interest at death and is revocable while the owner lives.

faqs.q: Does the beneficiary have to be told about the deed?
faqs.a: No. Section 15-15-402 says the beneficiary does not need to join in, sign, consent to or be notified of the deed before the owner dies. The beneficiary may still disclaim the property.

faqs.q: Does a will override a beneficiary deed in Colorado?
faqs.a: No. Under 15-15-405, a beneficiary deed that follows the statute cannot be revoked or changed by the owner's will. Revocation takes a recorded written instrument signed before death.

faqs.q: Can I sell my house if I recorded a beneficiary deed?
faqs.a: Yes. While you are alive the beneficiary has no interest, and you keep full authority over the property under 15-15-402 without anyone else's consent.

faqs.q: What if the beneficiary dies before the owner?
faqs.a: The statute says anti-lapse rules do not apply to beneficiary deeds, and if one of several beneficiaries dies first with no alternate named, that share goes to the surviving beneficiaries in proportion. A named successor grantee-beneficiary can be designated, so check how the deed was written.

faqs.q: How long do creditors have to make claims against a beneficiary deed property?
faqs.a: Creditor claims against the owner are barred one year after the owner's death under 15-15-411. Other claims by heirs or devisees are barred at the earlier of three years after death or one year after the death is recorded in the county.
